# The Word-Meaning Organ: Trained Encoder vs. Simple Ingestion + Machinery

## Bottom line up front
The literature does **not** support "word meaning = a single trained encoder that outputs a rich static vector." It supports a **two-system division of labor**: a comparatively simple, fast, hippocampal **indexing/binding** mechanism that ingests an arbitrary form-referent pairing in one or few trials, plus a slow cortical **consolidation** process that only over days/sleep cycles turns that index into something that behaves like a stable lexical/semantic entry (able to compete with neighbors, prime related concepts, generalize). Once cortically integrated, the "meaning" that gets read out is **not fixed** — it is reconstructed per-context by semantic control machinery. This is closer to your "simple ingestion + powerful surrounding machinery" model than to "one trained encoder," but the full picture requires acknowledging both a real hippocampal encoder (fast, sparse, pattern-completion-capable) and real cortical structure that stores something distributed and quasi-stable. **[ESTABLISHED framework; contested in its details, see below]**

---

## 1. How a new word's meaning is acquired

**Fast mapping — classic and modern status.** Carey & Bartlett (1978), the "chromium tray" study, showed preschoolers infer a novel word's referent from a single exposure using mutual-exclusivity/pragmatic inference, with partial retention a week later. **[ESTABLISHED]** as a developmental phenomenon in children.

Whether an analogous adult mechanism produces a *hippocampus-independent, direct-to-cortex* trace is **[CONTESTED, largely FAILED-REPLICATION]**. Coutanche & Thompson-Schill (2014, *J Exp Psychol Gen* 143(6):2296–2303) trained 50 participants on 16 novel animal-name pairings via fast mapping (FM) vs. explicit encoding (EE) and reported that FM produced near-immediate lexical competition effects that persisted overnight and let the new words prime semantically related concepts the next day — interpreted as rapid *cortical* integration bypassing normal hippocampal consolidation. This was extended to hippocampal-amnesia patients by **Sharon, Moscovitch & Gilboa (2011, PNAS)**: four amnesic patients with hippocampal damage performed at control levels learning novel word–picture pairs under FM instructions (relating the new item to a known, semantically related item) at both 10-minute and 1-week delays, while under standard explicit-encoding instructions they were impaired as expected — the striking claim being that a hippocampus-damaged brain could still acquire lexical-referent knowledge, just not via the normal declarative route.

Both claims have been substantially undermined by later work:
- **Warren & Duff (2014, *Hippocampus* 24:920–933)**, "Not so fast: Hippocampal amnesia slows word learning despite successful fast mapping" — severely amnesic patients (n=4), mildly amnesic (n=6), and controls (n=10) tested with online eye-movement measures found *no above-chance learning after two FM exposures* in amnesic patients, contradicting Sharon et al.'s claim of intact FM-based learning without hippocampus. **[FAILED-REPLICATION]**
- **Cooper, Greve & Henson (2019, *Cognitive Neuroscience* 10(4):196–209)**, "Little evidence for Fast Mapping (FM) in adults: A review and discussion," concluded that across the accumulated adult and amnesic-patient literature there is little solid evidence for FM as a *distinct*, hippocampus-independent learning mechanism at all; they and colleagues (Smith et al. 2014; Warren & Duff 2014) found no FM-specific benefit over explicit encoding for hippocampal-damage patients. A companion paper, **"Little evidence for fast mapping in adults with developmental amnesia"** (2019, *Cognitive Neuroscience*), reinforces this in a distinct amnesic population. **[FAILED-REPLICATION / CONTESTED — Cooper et al.'s own response to commentaries notes most commentators shared their skepticism, though not all.]**
- Directly on Coutanche & Thompson-Schill's cortical-integration claim: a 2023 paper in *Cognitive Neuropsychology* ("No evidence of fast mapping in healthy adults using an implicit memory measure: failures to replicate the lexical competition results of Coutanche and Thompson-Schill (2014)") reports failure to reproduce the original lexical-competition effect using an implicit measure. **[FAILED-REPLICATION]**

Net read: the *strong* version of the fast-mapping story (a genuinely separate, cortex-direct, hippocampus-independent encoding channel) has not survived replication. What survives is the weaker, CLS-consistent picture below.

**Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) account of word learning.** Davis & Gaskell (2009, *Phil Trans R Soc B* 364:3773–3800), "A complementary systems account of word learning: neural and behavioural evidence," lay out the division of labor explicitly: rapidly-acquired **episodic** representations of a new word-form and its context are stored via **medial temporal lobe / hippocampal** circuits from the first exposure; **lexical** integration — the new word competing with phonological neighbors during recognition, and its meaning becoming available for automatic/implicit access — depends on **slow neocortical learning**, which is why it lags behind the initial episodic trace by hours to days. This builds on the foundational McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly (1995) CLS theory (hippocampus = fast, sparse, pattern-separated; neocortex = slow, overlapping, interleaved, structure-extracting) and is updated for a machine-learning audience by **Kumaran, Hassabis & McClelland (2016, *Trends Cogn Sci* 20:512–534)**, "What Learning Systems do Intelligent Agents Need? Complementary Learning Systems Theory Updated," which explicitly reframes the hippocampal system as a fast episodic store whose role (crucial for the current question) is to support **replay-driven interleaving** so the slow cortical system avoids catastrophic interference while extracting generalizable structure. **[ESTABLISHED framework]**

Critically, this account says the hippocampal contribution to a *new word* is not "meaning" in any rich cortical-semantic sense; it is closer to a pointer to a specific episode/form (see indexing theory, §2). Meaning-proper — sense, associative structure, competitive lexical status — is a **cortical, slowly-trained** property. This is direct support for the "trained (slow) encoder + fast index" hybrid, not for "one trained encoder."

**Sleep/overnight consolidation.** Dumay & Gaskell (2007, *Psychol Sci* 18:35–39) is the founding demonstration: novel spoken words learned at 8pm showed no lexical-competition effect (inhibition of recognition of phonological neighbors) immediately, but did show it after a 12-hour interval containing sleep, and the effect persisted at 24h; words learned at 8am and tested after an equivalent waking interval showed no such competition. **[ESTABLISHED]** This has been replicated and extended by Tamminen, Bakker-Marshall, and others; a **2021 systematic review/meta-analysis in *Psychonomic Bulletin & Review*** ("The effect of sleep on novel word learning in healthy adults") pooling ~25 studies, 42 outcome measures, ~1,396 participants, found sleep benefits novel word learning with **g = 0.50** overall, g = 0.57 for recall, g = 0.52 for recognition — a real, moderate, and now well-replicated effect, though with documented boundary conditions (word-list length, recall vs. recognition format moderate effect size). **Bakker et al. (2015)** EEG work found N400 responses to new words shift from more MTL/hippocampal engagement pre-consolidation to more neocortical engagement post-consolidation — direct electrophysiological support for the CLS handoff. A useful further nuance from 2024 work (PMC11219009, "Consolidation improves the learning of new meanings for known words but not necessarily their integration into semantic memory") shows sleep helps *retention* of a new meaning even when it does not fully integrate that meaning into the existing semantic network — i.e., consolidation and semantic integration are separable processes, not one step. **[ESTABLISHED, with contested boundary conditions]**

What this means for the encoder question: if lexical competition — a signature of belonging to a trained, structured, mutually-inhibitory lexical-semantic system — literally does not exist until after a sleep-dependent, hours-to-days-long process, then **the "trained encoder" is not encoding at exposure time**. Exposure only writes an index/episodic trace. The rich, structured, competitive vector-like representation is built *later*, offline, by a slow consolidation process that looks like classic representation learning (interleaved replay extracting statistical structure) — which is a genuine encoder, just not the fast one that did the "ingestion."

**Hippocampal amnesia and word learning.** Beyond the FM controversy, broader amnesia work (Duff & Brown-Schmidt program) shows hippocampal-damage patients are impaired at forming *new* lexical-semantic knowledge and at flexible, creative, contextually-novel language use, but existing (pre-morbid) semantic memory is comparatively preserved — the classic Gabrieli/Bayley finding that profound amnesics can still slowly acquire some new semantic/factual knowledge over extended, repeated exposure (residual cortical learning, much slower than hippocampal-intact learning). **Duff & Brown-Schmidt (2012, "The hippocampus and the flexible use and processing of language")** argue hippocampus is recruited whenever language use requires flexible recombination/relational binding (e.g., establishing reference, common ground, using words in novel combinations) — not for routine access to already-consolidated word meanings. A 2020 ScienceDirect paper ("The limited role of hippocampal declarative memory in transient semantic activation during online language processing") explicitly argues hippocampal declarative memory contributes little to moment-to-moment semantic activation during normal comprehension — i.e., for *already known* words, hippocampus is largely bypassed; it matters for encoding new relational/lexical knowledge, not for running the encoder on familiar words. **[CONTESTED in the FM-specific claims, but ESTABLISHED that hippocampus is selectively necessary for new/flexible lexical-relational binding, not for accessing already-consolidated meaning.]**

---

## 2. The hippocampal machinery

**CA3 pattern completion / DG pattern separation.** Treves & Rolls (1992, 1994) modeled CA3 as a sparse auto-associative recurrent network with an estimated capacity on the order of **~36,000 patterns** given rodent CA3 connectivity — a quantitative account of how a small store can support completion from partial cues. **[ESTABLISHED theoretical framework, still cited]**. Direct physiological evidence: **Neunuebel & Knierim (2014, *Neuron* 81:416–427)**, "CA3 retrieves coherent representations from degraded input," recorded single units in DG and CA3 while morphing the environment continuously and found DG activity changed abruptly/nonlinearly with small environmental changes (pattern **separation**), while CA3 output stayed closer to the originally stored representation than its degraded DG input (pattern **completion**) — direct, quantitative single-unit evidence for the classic computational division of labor. **[ESTABLISHED]**. Complementary optical/behavioral work (Yassa & Stark 2011, *Trends Neurosci* 34:515–525, "Pattern separation in the hippocampus") established DG's role in human behavioral pattern separation via high-resolution fMRI mnemonic similarity tasks; this remains dominant though not unchallenged (some argue for a "binding" rather than pure-separation account of DG). **[ESTABLISHED core claim; some CONTESTED alternative framings]**

**Indexing theory — the frame most directly relevant to your question.** Teyler & DiScenna's original theory and its update, **Teyler & Rudy (2007, *Hippocampus* 17:1158–1169)**, propose explicitly that "the hippocampus itself does not contain the content of an experience but it does provide an index that allows the content to be retrieved" — a sparse pointer into distributed neocortical activity patterns, not a copy of the content. **[ESTABLISHED as an influential theoretical frame]**. This has a modern, mechanistic revival: **Goode, Tanaka, Sahay & McHugh (2020, *Neuron* 107:805–820)**, "An Integrated Index: Engrams, Place Cells, and Hippocampal Memory," reviews contemporary engram, place-cell, and circuit evidence and argues hippocampal engram ensembles function precisely as the indexing theory predicted: they route/reinstate distributed cortical (and other hippocampal/extrahippocampal) activity rather than storing semantic content themselves, and identifies specific molecular/circuit determinants (e.g., engram cell allocation biases, inhibitory microcircuits) governing this indexing function. **[ESTABLISHED-CONTESTED — a coherent, mechanistically grounded modern instantiation of indexing theory, but it remains a synthesis/review position, not a single decisive experiment, and the "binding vs. separation" debate about DG (above) shows this area of hippocampal theory is still actively contested.]**

This is squarely in favor of your "simple ingestion mechanism" framing: the hippocampal contribution to a new word is best described as a sparse index/pointer allocated fast (potentially one-shot, via CA3 completion/DG separation dynamics), not a rich trained semantic embedding. The *rich* representation, if and when it exists, lives distributed in cortex and is only *reconstructed via* the hippocampal index during early retrieval, with the index itself eventually becoming dispensable as cortico-cortical connections strengthen (systems consolidation).

---

## 3. Is cortical semantic representation itself simple, with richness from machinery?

**Yee & Thompson-Schill (2016, *Psychon Bull Rev* 23(4):1015–1027), "Putting concepts into context."** This is the load-bearing paper you asked about. Their actual argument, reviewed across multiple timescales, is **not** "there is no stored representation," but that conceptual *activation* is graded and context-modulated at every level: long-term experience (frequency/associative history shifts feature weighting), recent experience (priming/adaptation), current task goals (top-down control selectively amplifying task-relevant features — citing their own and others' work showing selective retrieval of, e.g., functional vs. perceptual features of the same object depending on task), and even the moment-to-moment unfolding of a single retrieval act (early activation of concept-general/dominant features, later narrowing to context-specific features, evidenced by TMS/ERP/eye-tracking timecourse studies from the Thompson-Schill lab and others). Their evidence is behavioral (feature-verification RT context effects), neural (LIFG/semantic-control recruitment scaling with need for selection among competing features — this literature is anchored to Thompson-Schill's long line of work implicating left inferior frontal gyrus in *selection* among activated-but-competing semantic representations, not in storage), and developmental/associative (context effects present even in young children). **The argument is that the "concept" is a *retrieval event* shaped jointly by a stored associative/distributional substrate and by control processes that determine which parts of it get activated and how strongly — not that there is no substrate.** **[ESTABLISHED, well-evidenced, but note: this is a claim about flexible *access*, not proof that the underlying stored substrate is low-dimensional/simple — that stronger claim is a further inference, not directly demonstrated by their data.]**

**Casasanto & Lupyan (2015), "All concepts are ad hoc concepts"** (in *The Conceptual Mind*, MIT Press) push further, arguing there is no such thing as a context-independent stored concept at all — every instantiation is constructed on the fly from contextual cues, and apparent stability is just overlap across similar contexts of use. This is a **stronger, more theoretical/philosophical claim** than Yee & Thompson-Schill's, drawing on relevant-feature variability across linguistic/cultural contexts (color concepts, spatial terms, category-boundary shifts by task) rather than new quantitative data of its own. **[CONTESTED / theoretical position — influential but more programmatic than the Yee & Thompson-Schill evidence review; not universally accepted.]**

**Hoffman, McClelland & Lambon Ralph (2018, *Psychol Rev* 125:293–328), "Concepts, control and context."** This is the best-specified computational instantiation of the "machinery matters as much as representation" view. Their model combines a **hub-and-spoke** distributed representation (anterior temporal lobe hub integrating modality-specific spokes) with a **prefrontal control system** that dynamically biases retrieval toward context-relevant features, and a recurrent buffer letting prior context shape ongoing activation. Crucially, they show computationally that the *same* stored hub-and-spoke weights, combined with different control settings, reproduce context-dependent behavior (e.g., typicality effects, category-specific and modality-specific semantic deficits after damage, context-dependent feature weighting) that would otherwise look like the representation itself changing. This directly supports the "moderate substrate + heavy-lifting control machinery" architecture: representation is real and distributed but comparatively low-complexity/associative, while flexible, rich, context-appropriate *behavior* comes from the semantic control system (PFC/ATL-adjacent) doing selective gating. **[ESTABLISHED, computationally grounded]**

**Counter-case (stable, context-invariant representation doing real work).** The retrofitting/counter-fitting/LEAR literature (§4c) is itself part of the counter-case: it only makes sense to inject synonym/antonym/hypernymy *constraints* into a vector space if there is a genuine, stable lexical-relational structure that distributional/contextual statistics alone under-determine — i.e., word meaning has a component that is not simply "whatever the current retrieval context computes" but a standing relational fact (dog IS-A animal; hot is the antonym, not the synonym, of cold) that must be represented explicitly and persistently to be used correctly. Additionally, decades of semantic-priming, feature-norm (e.g., McRae et al.), and patient (semantic dementia — profound, graceful degradation of a *stored* semantic representation as ATL atrophies, per Lambon Ralph's semantic dementia work) literatures support a genuine, damageable, distributed but reasonably stable cortical store — context modulates access to it, but doesn't manufacture it from nothing every time. **[ESTABLISHED]**

---

## 4. Computational/ML evidence

**(a) Retrieval-augmented vs. parametric.** Lewis et al. 2020 RAG (the seminal comparison, referenced in current surveys) found retrieval-augmented generation produces more specific, diverse, and factual output than parametric-only baselines on knowledge-intensive tasks, but a persistent gap remains vs. closed-book (fully parametric) performance in some settings — i.e., neither pure retrieval nor pure parametric dominates; the state of the art blends both, mirroring the biological hippocampal-index-plus-cortical-store split. **[ESTABLISHED, actively evolving 2023-2026 literature on RAG vs. fine-tuning trade-offs — fine-tuning integrates knowledge into parameters but is prompt-sensitive and forgetting-prone; RAG is current/updatable but retrieval-quality-bounded.]**

**(b) Count-based/PPMI vs. trained dense embeddings.** **Levy, Goldberg & Dagan (2015, *TACL* 3:211–225), "Improving Distributional Similarity with Lessons Learned from Word Embeddings"** — the key finding is that most of the *apparent* superiority of neural embeddings (SGNS/word2vec, GloVe) over classical count-based PPMI+SVD distributional vectors is attributable to **hyperparameter and design choices** (context window, negative sampling as implicit shifted-PMI weighting, subsampling, vector normalization) that can be, and were, transferred onto the classical count-based methods. Once those hyperparameters are matched, "there is no consistent significant advantage of one approach over the other" — Levy & Goldberg's related theoretical result (Levy & Goldberg 2014, "Neural word embedding as implicit matrix factorization") shows SGNS is mathematically implicitly factorizing a shifted-PMI matrix, i.e., **the same object a count-based method builds explicitly.** **[ESTABLISHED]** This directly supports your case (c)/(b): a simple, transparent, count-based/explicit-feature representation, properly engineered, is essentially performance-equivalent to a "trained" dense encoder for general similarity/analogy — the encoder isn't doing anything the counts couldn't also do.

**(c) Dense embeddings fail to separate synonyms from antonyms — this is the strongest, most load-bearing empirical result for your question, and I retrieved the exact numbers.** Standard distributional/trained embeddings conflate similarity and relatedness/substitutability, so antonyms (which occur in nearly identical contexts — "hot"/"cold") end up with high cosine similarity, indistinguishable from true synonyms. On **SimLex-999** (Hill, Reichart & Korhonen 2015, *Comput Linguistics* 41(4):665–695 — genuine-similarity, not relatedness, gold standard, human inter-annotator agreement ≈0.67), from the **Mrkšić et al. (2016, "Counter-fitting Word Vectors to Linguistic Constraints," arXiv:1603.00892) Table 2 numbers I pulled directly**:
- **GloVe baseline: 0.41 Spearman**
- **GloVe + retrofitting (Faruqui et al. 2015): 0.53**
- **GloVe + counter-fitting (Mrkšić et al. 2016): 0.58**
- **Paragram-SL999 baseline: 0.69**
- **Paragram-SL999 + retrofitting: 0.68** (no gain — retrofitting doesn't help an already-specialized space)
- **Paragram-SL999 + counter-fitting: 0.74** (new SOTA at the time, above human inter-annotator agreement of 0.67)

**[ESTABLISHED, exact numbers verified]**. The pattern is unambiguous: raw trained/distributional embeddings (GloVe 0.41) are mediocre at genuine similarity because they cannot distinguish antonymy from synonymy; injecting **external explicit relational knowledge** (WordNet/PPDB synonym+antonym constraints — i.e., structured facts, not more training data or bigger models) produces the largest single jump in performance (0.41→0.58, a 41% relative gain from GloVe; 0.41→0.74 combining Paragram's better base training + counter-fitting, an 80% relative gain). **Vulić & Mrkšić (2018, NAACL, "Specialising Word Vectors for Lexical Entailment," LEAR)** extend this to asymmetric hyponymy/entailment relations (IS-A), again via explicit constraint injection (attract-repel framework) rather than more distributional training, achieving further state-of-the-art gains on HyperLex and graded lexical entailment. This is a clean, numbers-backed demonstration that **knowledge injection (explicit relational facts) beats scale/training alone for fine-grained lexical distinctions** — directly answering (d) as well: the 2020s knowledge-graph-injection and structured-fine-tuning literature (e.g., ScienceDirect 2024 comparative analysis of knowledge-injection strategies, arXiv 2508.14427 KG-infused fine-tuning) continues this pattern, generally finding structured knowledge injection outperforms scale-only approaches specifically on fine-grained/relational distinctions, even as pure scale continues to win on broad coverage. **[ESTABLISHED for (c); the 2023-2026 LLM-era literature on (d) is real but more fragmented/CONTESTED in its specific comparisons since apples-to-apples fine-grained lexical benchmarks are less standardized than SimLex-999 was for embeddings.]**

---

## Synthesis

Every strand converges on the same architecture: **fast, low-dimensional, arbitrary-binding capacity (hippocampal index/CA3 completion) ingests a new word-referent pairing essentially immediately; a slow, offline, sleep-gated cortical process (CLS "slow learner") is what builds anything resembling a structured, competitive, trained representation; and even once built, that representation is not queried as a static vector but is actively, selectively reconstructed by prefrontal/ATL semantic-control machinery per context.** The ML evidence reinforces this from the opposite direction: a "trained encoder" alone (GloVe/SGNS) is demonstrably *not* sufficient for fine-grained lexical distinctions (SimLex-999 0.41) — what closes most of the gap to human performance is injecting explicit relational structure (0.41→0.74), i.e., machinery/knowledge external to the raw trained embedding, not more/better training of the embedding itself. The FM literature's replication collapse specifically kills the strongest version of "one-shot trained cortical encoder"; what remains standing is indexing + slow consolidation + control, which is your hypothesis, not the trained-encoder-alone hypothesis.
